newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate approves two top Justice jobs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate approves two top Justice jobs.

text.p: The Senate overwhelmingly approved Thursday President Clinton's nominees for two top positions at the Department of Justice, where a half-dozen senior posts have been vacant.

Eric Holder, 46, a respected Washington prosecutor, won a 100-0 confirmation vote to become the number two official in the Justice Department under Attorney General Janet Reno. He will be the highest-ranking black ever in the department.
His confirmation had been delayed in part because of opposition to the second nominee, Joel Klein for assistant attorney general for the antitrust division.

Only a handful of senators opposed Klein for a telecommunications antitrust decision he had made, but they did slow down the confirmation process. He ended up being confirmed 88-12, with the no votes all coming from Democrats.
Calling the two officials "distinguished public servants," Reno in a statement said, "This is a good day for the American people, for law enforcement and for the cause of justice."

Holder, 46, was the U.S. attorney for Washington, the city's top prosecutor for federal crimes. He has also worked in the Justice Department's elite Public Integrity Section, specialising in public corruption cases. In 1988 President Ronald Reagan named him a judge on D.C. Superior Court, which handles local cases.
He has also had a high profile in community service, including a role in a mentoring group called Concerned Black Men.
"Eric has a wealth of experience on which he can draw. Eric will continue leading the fight to safeguard our streets and neighbourhoods," Reno said.

Klein's chief critic, Sen. Ernest Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat, said that Klein was not using tough enough standards to evaluate telecommunications mergers. Klein has been acting antitrust chief since Ann Bingaman resigned last November, and Hollings objected to Klein's approval of Bell Atlantic Corp.'s aquisition of Nynex Corp.

Another critic, Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democrat, urged Klein to use a "no-nonsense standard" in future telecommunications mergers and acquisitions or else "everybody who uses a telephone" will face higher prices.

The opponents of the Clinton-appointee were all Democrats who wanted a tougher regulatory stance under the new telecommunications law, which is supposed to foster industry competition instead of consolidation.
The confirmations fill in two of the seven gaps at the top of the Justice Department, created as officials stepped down during Clinton's second term.

Clinton recently nominated Raymond Fisher to be associate attorney general, Bill Lee to head up its civil rights division and Beth Nolan to run the office of legal counsel. He has not yet selected an assistant attorney general for the criminal division.
The seventh vacancy occurred this week when Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger, the Clinton administration's top courtroom lawyer, announced he plans to leave next month.
